title: OIDC Refresh Token Grant (with Rotation)
subtitle: How a SPA renews an expired access token without sending the user back through login — and how rotation plus reuse-detection catches a stolen token.

steps.label: Access token has expired
steps.lede: The user is already signed in, but the short-lived access token (AT1) has expired. The public client (SPA) still holds a refresh token from the original grant and will use it to get a fresh access token silently.
steps.devtools: Open DevTools → Network, enable Preserve log, and filter Fetch/XHR with token in the box. For a public client (SPA) the refresh runs in the browser and is fully visible; for a confidential/BFF client it would be a back-channel call you’d only see in backend logs.

steps.label: Send the refresh request
steps.lede: The client posts grant_type=refresh_token with the stored refresh token. A public client identifies itself with client_id (no secret); the browser is the origin.
steps.devtools: Open the Payload tab and confirm grant_type=refresh_token and the refresh_token being sent (rt_synthetic_A1_0000). Note the value — you’ll compare it against the one that comes back. A confidential client would instead send an Authorization: Basic header or a client_assertion on the back channel.

steps.label: Rotated tokens returned
steps.lede: The IdP validates the refresh token, then rotates it: it invalidates the one you sent and returns a brand-new refresh token (same family) alongside a fresh access token and a re-issued ID token.

jwt.title: Decoded re-issued id_token
payload: Stable opaque user id (unchanged across refreshes)
NEW expiry — later than the previous token
NEW issued-at — the moment of this refresh
UNCHANGED — the original login, not now

steps.devtools: In the Response, confirm the refresh_token differs from the one you sent (…A2_0001 vs …A1_0000) — that is rotation. The client must now store the new one and discard the old. In the id_token, iat/exp move forward but auth_time stays pinned to the original login: a refresh renews tokens, it does not re-authenticate the user. There is no nonce (no front-channel /authorize).

steps.label: Call the API with the fresh token
steps.lede: The client retries the resource call, now presenting the freshly minted access token as a Bearer credential.
steps.devtools: Confirm the Authorization: Bearer header carries the new access token, not the expired one. The resource server validates it (signature via JWKS, iss, aud, exp, scopes) before returning data.

steps.label: Reuse detection: old token replayed
steps.lede: If the already-rotated token (…A1_0000) is replayed — typically by an attacker who stole it — the IdP sees a used token, treats it as a breach, and revokes the entire token family.
steps.devtools: This shows as a red 400 on the token request with error=invalid_grant. Because the AS revokes the whole family, the next refresh — even with the current …A2_0001 token — will also fail, forcing interactive re-authentication. That is the point: a stolen refresh token cannot be used silently for long.

steps.label: Re-authentication required
steps.lede: With the family revoked, the client can no longer refresh. It falls back to sending the user through an interactive login at /authorize.
steps.devtools: Nothing more to refresh. Other benign reasons a refresh returns invalid_grant: the family hit its sliding idle window or absolute lifetime. In all cases the client redirects to /authorize for a fresh login. Scope on refresh may only narrow the grant, never widen it.
